operations.text: SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
Recycling Service Pilot Implementation
This document sets out how the recycling service pilot will be implemented across
the participating collection sites, from mobilisation through review. It defines the
operating scope, the duties of the delivery team, the evidence that will be
gathered and the questions the review must answer. The pilot runs for 12 weeks
and is treated as a learning exercise: observations are recorded separately from
any causal claims about household behaviour or material recovery.
Pilot Purpose and Operating Scope
The pilot tests whether a revised collection and sorting arrangement can be
delivered reliably at the participating sites within the agreed service window.
Scope covers kerbside set-out, transfer to the sorting point, contamination checks
and resident communication. Activities outside this scope, including permanent
fleet procurement and long-term contract changes, are excluded and will be
considered only after the review reports its findings to the sponsoring committee.
Service Model and Collection Routes
The service model uses a fixed weekly route pattern with two collection passes
per site and a shared transfer point. Route sequencing was chosen to keep
vehicle dwell time short and to allow sorting staff to receive material in consistent
batches. Route supervisors record arrival and departure times at each stop so
that the review can compare planned and actual service delivery without
attributing differences to any single cause.
Site Readiness and Equipment
Each site must be confirmed ready before collections begin. Readiness covers bin
placement, signage, access for collection vehicles, staff briefing and a dry sorting
area. Site leads sign a readiness checklist and report exceptions to the pilot
coordinator, who decides whether a site starts on schedule or joins in a later
wave. Equipment shortfalls are logged and resolved before the first collection
pass.
Bin Allocation and Resident Communication
Bin allocation follows household size bands agreed with site leads, and every
household receives a short printed guide in plain language. Communication
covers set-out times, accepted materials and what happens when a bin is
rejected. Residents can raise questions through a local phone line, with responses
targeted within 2 working days. Messages are kept consistent across sites so that
the review can compare experiences fairly.

Contamination Checks at Set-Out
Collection crews carry out a visual contamination check at set-out and tag bins
that contain clearly non-accepted material. Tagged bins are recorded with a
reason code and left for the household to correct before the next pass. Crews do
not open sealed bags. The check is a service quality measure, not an
enforcement action, and households receive a follow-up note explaining the
correction needed.

Figure 1: Contamination tag reason codes
Sorting Point Intake Records
The sorting point keeps an intake record for every batch, noting arrival time,
source site, estimated weight band and visible contamination. Records are
entered on the same day and cross-checked by a second staff member. Where a
batch is held back for inspection, the reason is written on the record. These
entries form the main evidence base for the review and are retained for the full
pilot period.

Temporary Site Adjustments
Site leads may request temporary adjustments, such as a moved collection point

or an extra bin, when access or weather conditions require it. Requests are
submitted in writing and approved by the pilot coordinator within 5 working days.
Approved adjustments are logged with the date, reason and expected duration so
that the review can distinguish planned service design from short-term
operational fixes.
Route Contingency Arrangements
When a route cannot be completed, the supervisor activates a contingency plan
that prioritises households missed on the previous pass and defers non-urgent
transfers. Affected residents are notified the same day through the local phone
line and printed notice where needed. Each activation is recorded with the
trigger, the stops affected and the recovery date, allowing the review to assess
how often contingency arrangements were needed.
Site Readiness Evidence and Checks
Readiness evidence is collected through signed checklists, photographs of bin
placement and brief notes from site briefings. The coordinator samples completed
checklists to confirm that entries are consistent and that exceptions were
resolved. Evidence is filed by site and week, so that any later question about a
site's starting condition can be answered from the record rather than from
recollection.
Monitoring, Records and Reporting
Monitoring combines route logs, sorting point intake records and resident contact
notes. The pilot coordinator compiles a short weekly summary for the delivery
team and a fuller report at the end of the pilot. Records are kept in a single
shared register with clear ownership, and any gap is flagged at the next weekly
meeting so that it can be corrected while the relevant staff are still available.

Sampling and Observation Method
Observation uses a structured sampling approach across the participating sites,
with checks spread over the pilot period rather than concentrated in one week.
Observers follow a written checklist and record what they see without inferring
household intent. Simulated observations are labelled as such in the register, and
the review team is instructed not to treat observed associations as evidence of
cause and effect.
Data Handling and Quality Assurance
Data handling follows a simple rule: one entry, one owner, one date. The register
is reviewed weekly for missing fields, duplicate batch records and inconsistent
reason codes. A second reviewer checks a sample of entries against paper forms.
Corrections are made by annotation rather than deletion, so that the review can
see what changed and why, and the audit trail remains intact.
Supporting records are presented in Table 3.
Table 3: Quality assurance checks on register entries
Weekly Summary and Escalation
Each week the coordinator issues a short summary covering collections
completed, tagged bins, held batches and open resident questions. Issues that
affect safety or service continuity are escalated to the sponsoring committee

immediately rather than waiting for the weekly cycle. The summary is
deliberately brief so that the delivery team reads it, and detailed figures remain
in the register for the final review.
Observation Log and Sample Coverage
The observation log records what was seen at each check, the time, the site and
the observer. Coverage is tracked against the planned sample so that
under-observed periods are visible early. The table below summarises the
planned observation schedule and the type of evidence each check produces,
distinguishing recorded observations from later interpretation by the review
team.

Record Gaps and Follow-Up Actions
When a record is missing, the coordinator raises a follow-up action with a named
owner and a due date. Actions are closed only when the missing entry is restored
or the gap is explained in writing. Recurring gaps are discussed at the weekly
meeting, since they often point to a form design problem or an unclear duty
rather than to individual error.
Interpreting Observed Patterns
Observed patterns, such as a rise in tagged bins during a particular week, are
reported as observations and not as proof that a communication change caused
the difference. The review team compares records across sites and weeks, notes
plausible alternative explanations and states clearly where the evidence is too
thin to support any conclusion about cause.
Review Questions for the Final Report
The final report must answer a fixed set of questions: whether the service ran as
designed, where records were incomplete, which adjustments were needed and
what residents asked about most often. It must also state what the pilot cannot
tell us, particularly about long-term behaviour change. Recommendations are

separated from findings so that decision-makers can see the basis for each
proposal.
Reporting Calendar and Responsibilities
Reporting follows a fixed calendar: weekly summaries during delivery, a mid-pilot
checkpoint and a final report after the last collection. The coordinator owns the
calendar, site leads supply site records and the review team drafts findings.
Drafts are circulated for correction before publication, and the final report is
presented to the sponsoring committee with the underlying register attached.
